newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major faces new battles over Europe.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major faces new battles over Europe.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major suffered an embarrassing defeat over Europe on Wednesday when members of parliament rejected government plans to avoid a full-scale debate on the crucial issue of the European single currency.

The defeat in a parliamentary committee came as the opposition Labour party stepped up its attacks, sensing Major's dwindling parliamentary majority could put the government under increasing pressure in the months leading to an election.

"Few issues have raised public concern in Britain as much as the single currency...yet it seems this government is seeking to avoid some of the more important issues being debated," Labour Treasury spokesman Mike O'Brien said.
The government signalled it intended to ignore the embarrassing defeat in the parliamentary committee which studies European legislation.
But it is likely to come under increasing pressure to hold a full parliamentary debate despite its fears this could reopen the chronic divisions in the ruling party over Europe.
More than 150 members of parliament from all parties have signed a motion calling on the government to bow to demands for a debate open to all 651 members of the House of Commons.
Both Labour and the Conservatives have promised a referendum before they would take Britain into a single currency.

But Labour argues that it is committed to Europe and will make a decision based on economic criteria while it says Major is a hostage to members of his own party bitterly opposed to any moves towards European integration.
The committee rejected by seven votes to six a government motion asking it to "take note" of three documents on EMU.
One was on the creation of a new exchange rate mechanism, another on a stability pact to ensure budgetary discipline in a single currency and a third on rules for the new Euro currency.

The government was defeated when former former Conservative ministerial aide John Whittingdale sided with the opposition which was angry at the lack of parliamentary time available to scrutinise the documents and demanded a full debate.
Labour business managers called the defeat unprecedented and vowed to try to force a full-scale debate on Europe.
And Labour's foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook said in a speech to parliamentary journalists that Major was making a huge mistake in trying to win over voters by waging war on Europe.
"It is wild fantasy, though, to imagine the Conservatives can achieve a general election breakthrough... by launching a jihad against Brussels," Cook said.
Major -- lagging far behind in opinion polls and with a parliamentary majority of just one with byelections pending -- must call an election by May at the latest.
But on Wednesday he defiantly rejected suggestions he could be forced into an early election by his dwindline majority.
"I think we will be able to pick our own election date," Major told the domestic Press Association news agency.
